headline: Shared filesystem and write access create medium prompt-injection, leakage, and conflict risks; no documented pairwise isolation reduces confidence.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can read/write filesystem and use MCP; Agent B reads/writes documents in a container. If B processes A-written files or A ingests B outputs from the shared workspace, malicious document content can steer downstream prompts. The pairwise bridge is plausible from both profiles, though not explicitly documented.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes files produced by agent_a without content sanitization
IF agent_a loads document text from the shared workspace as instructions
mitigations: Separate work directories per agent
Strip instruction-like text from exchanged documents
Require explicit allowlist for files passed between agents
Add provenance tags to all handoffs
requires-engineering: enforce parser-level content isolation

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches application context and handles model provider API keys/plugin credentials, while Agent B processes documents, images, and text. Because both have filesystem access and A has broad network egress, sensitive document content could flow from B into A’s outputs or external APIs if they share files or context. The profiles do not show default isolation between them.
conditions: IF both agents share a workspace containing sensitive documents
IF agent_a forwards loaded context to external model APIs
mitigations: Use separate encrypted workspaces
Block sensitive files from agent_a inputs
Disable external egress for sensitive runs
Redact secrets before handoff
requires-engineering: add DLP scanning on shared files

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem and support multiple instances, so concurrent modification of shared files is plausible. Agent A’s session-scoped shared state via memory store and Agent B’s containerized execution do not prove locking, so race conditions or overwrite conflicts remain possible in default orchestration.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or file set
IF the orchestrator does not provide file locks or transactional updates
mitigations: Assign disjoint output paths
Serialize writes with a simple lock file
Make one agent read-only for shared artifacts
Snapshot inputs before processing
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can produce transformed context or tool outputs, and Agent B is a document-processing pipeline that may treat incoming text as authoritative extraction input. Without an explicit verification step, A’s errors can cascade into B’s parsed outputs or downstream actions. The profiles show a plausible handoff but no built-in cross-checking.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a output as source text without verification
IF downstream systems act on B’s extracted results
mitigations: Insert a human review step for handoffs
Compare extracted fields against source documents
Require confidence thresholds before action
Log provenance for each extracted claim
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A handles model-provider API keys and plugin credentials, while Agent B processes documents and images under a container. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so compliance risk is limited to documented gaps in retention or data handling rather than a clear breach pathway. Only A is cited because the issue is its secret-handling surface.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into agent_a secrets or prompts
IF retention policies differ for the same document class
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in secrets fields
Review retention settings before deployment
Keep regulated documents out of shared workspaces
Document data-class handling rules
requires-engineering: formalize residency and retention controls
